Assessment & Plan (Integrating DDx)
- Acute reaction after bee/wasp sting to arm with localized erythema and puncture mark; no objective airway compromise on video exam.
- Most consistent with a localized allergic/inflammatory reaction to Hymenoptera sting (high likelihood per DDx).
- Early anaphylaxis considered less likely given absence of visible lip/tongue swelling, normal breathing/speech, and no systemic features (moderate concern only; safety-netting provided).
- Anxiety/panic may be contributing to subjective dyspnea (moderate likelihood per DDx).
- Early cellulitis unlikely given onset within minutes and lack of warmth/spreading erythema (low likelihood); monitor for evolving infection.

Management Plan
- Start antihistamine: chlorphenamine (Piriton) 4 mg tablet up to 6 times daily; route not documented. Alternatively, a once-daily antihistamine (specific agent/dose not documented).
- Safety net: Seek urgent care/ER immediately if any breathing difficulty, progressive lip/tongue/throat swelling, stridor, voice change, generalized hives, vomiting, dizziness/syncope, or rapid symptom progression.
- Local care: Monitor sting site for spreading redness, warmth, increasing pain, or fever; if signs of local infection develop, consider antibiotic.
- Follow-up: If symptoms worsen, persist, or if similar reactions recur, reconsult; allergy testing/blood tests may be considered if reactions become recurrent (per discussion).
- Patient provided education on anaphylaxis warning signs.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx):
- Localized allergic/inflammatory reaction to Hymenoptera sting – High likelihood: Immediate local erythema with puncture mark; no objective airway involvement.
- Early anaphylaxis – Moderate likelihood: Temporal association with sting and subjective dyspnea/oral sensations, but no objective signs and stable exam.
- Anxiety/panic-related dyspnea – Moderate likelihood: Normal observed respiration and history of panic; sought reassurance.
